Based on the retrieved matches, it appears that the insertion allele of the ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) gene I/D polymorphism is indeed a candidate gene for insulin resistance.

The ACE DD genotype has been found to be associated with increased sensitivity in non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM) subjects. This suggests that the ACE DD genotype may play a role in mediating the association between plasma glucose levels and cardiovascular risk, which is not solely explained by insulin resistance.

Furthermore, studies have shown that individuals with the ACE DD genotype are at increased risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD) among hypertensive patients, indicating that genetic factors may contribute to the development of CKD.

Additionally, a high cumulative dose of regular insulin has been linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis, suggesting that genetic predispositions can influence cardiovascular health.

While there is some controversy regarding the association between ACE gene polymorphisms and schizophrenia (as suggested by Prompt 8), more recent studies have found that variants at HINT1 may be associated with schizophrenia, particularly when examined in combination with other genes. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings.

Overall, the available evidence suggests that the insertion allele of the ACE gene I/D polymorphism is indeed a candidate gene for insulin resistance and may also contribute to an increased risk of CKD among hypertensive patients.
